summary:
Daniel opens in 605 BC: Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon besieges Jerusalem and carries off temple treasure and young Judean nobles — among them Daniel and his three friends, retrained in "the language and literature of the Chaldeans" and renamed Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego (1:1–7). Their court stories fill chapters 1–6; Daniel's visions, 7–12. The book is also bilingual: Aramaic, the era's international language, runs from 2:4 through chapter 7, with Hebrew on either side.

The stories share one refrain: "the Most High rules over the kingdom of mankind and gives it to whom He wishes" (4:17). A ten-day test of vegetables and water lets the four refuse the royal food (1). Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron, and clay — a succession of kingdoms — shattered by a stone "cut out, but not by human hands" that becomes a mountain: God's kingdom, which "will never be destroyed" (2). Refusing the king's golden statue — "we will not serve your gods" (3:18) — the three friends walk through the furnace unharmed beside a fourth figure who "looks like a son of the gods" (3:25). Nebuchadnezzar is driven out to eat grass like an ox until he honors the Most High (4); Belshazzar drinks from the Jerusalem temple's vessels while a hand writes MENE, MENE, TEKEL, PARSIN on the wall — translated in the text: numbered, weighed, divided (5:26–28) — and is slain that night; under Darius the Mede, Daniel prays "toward Jerusalem" three times a day and survives the den of lions (6).

The visions are apocalyptic (Greek for "unveiling"): four beasts rise from the sea — winged lion, bear, four-headed leopard, a fourth with iron teeth — four kingdoms again. Then "the Ancient of Days" takes His seat, and "One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven" receives "an everlasting dominion that will not pass away" (7:9–14). "Son of Man" is Jesus' most frequent name for Himself, and He answers the high priest at His trial with this scene (Matthew 26:64). A ram and a goat follow, decoded within the vision as Media-Persia and Greece (8:20–21). Reading in Jeremiah that Jerusalem's desolation would last seventy years (9:2), Daniel prays; the angel Gabriel answers with "seventy weeks" (9:24), reckoned by interpreters in widely different ways.

The final vision (10–12) traces wars between kings of the North and South — detail most scholars link to the Greek dynasties after Alexander, down to the temple's desecration under Antiochus IV in 167 BC. It ends past death: "many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt" (12:2) — often called the Old Testament's plainest statement of resurrection. Hence the debate over the book's date: the traditional view takes it as sixth-century prophecy given far in advance; many modern scholars date its final form to the 100s BC. Daniel himself is told to seal the book "until the time of the end" (12:4) and given a closing promise: "You will rest, and then you will arise to your inheritance at the end of the days" (12:13).
